slides.title: In 897, a pope dug up a dead pope and put him on trial.
Dead about nine months
slides.body: Pope Stephen VI had the corpse of Pope Formosus dug up, dressed in papal vestments and seated on a throne in Rome's Lateran basilica to stand trial.

slides.title: A deacon spoke for the corpse
slides.body: The charges came from church law: perjury, moving from the see of Porto to Rome, and acting as a bishop while reduced to lay status.

slides.title: Verdict: guilty
slides.body: The corpse was stripped of its vestments and of the three fingers of its right hand used in blessing. Then it was thrown into the Tiber.

slides.title: It was about politics
slides.body: Formosus had crowned Arnulf of Carinthia emperor in 896, against the rival house of Spoleto. Who pushed for the trial is still debated.

slides.title: Months later, it was his turn
slides.body: That summer Stephen VI was deposed and strangled in prison. Formosus was reburied in St Peter's, and in 898 Pope John IX banned trials of the dead.

caption: The defendant had been dead about nine months, and he still lost. Which detail is the worst: the throne, the fingers or the river?
xPost: In 897 a pope had a dead pope dug up, dressed in vestments, put on a throne and tried. A deacon spoke for the corpse. Guilty: it lost three fingers and went into the Tiber. Months later the pope who staged it was strangled in prison.
